steps.text: **Development** means bringing your pieces off their first squares to places where they do something. A **tempo** is one move of time. If you spent your moves on pieces and the opponent spent his on other things, you hold a **lead**. This lesson teaches you to count a lead, use it, notice when it is gone, and build it or defend against it.

**Why a lead matters.** A piece at home can neither attack nor defend. Where the fight begins, the side with more pieces out has more of them there, and the other side has fewer defenders and fewer attackers. Edward Lasker's rule of thumb, which I restate in my own words from his *Chess Strategy*: a lead in development permits an attack, and a deficit forbids one. Look at f7 on the first board and ask who can reach it.

steps.text: **How to count.** Count the pieces off their first squares that do something, plus castling. Pawn moves are not counted themselves; they matter only because they let a piece count. A piece that moves twice has spent a move for no new job, and the early queen often does too. [I] These are habits with exceptions: you will see an early queen work in the real game below. Nimzowitsch argued that development belongs to the whole army, so [I] a stuck rook counts too.

steps.chapter: Why it works, and when it fails

steps.text: The shot worked for three reasons you can check beforehand. Your pieces can reach the target quickly. The target has few developed defenders: here only the king. And giving up a piece drags the king into the open, where the knight check wins a second piece. Remove one reason and the sacrifice can lose a piece: the look-alike a few boards on shows it. [I] I expect that to hold more often than not, but I have not counted.

steps.text: A lead is a chance, not a promise. It stops working when a developed piece guards the target, when the king has a safe square, when the opponent can trade your attackers, or when you wait and the lead shrinks. [I] A locked centre probably slows an attack because the lines stay shut; this lesson does not test it. Before sacrificing, ask: *what has changed since the last time this worked?* The next pair of positions changes exactly one thing.

steps.text: **Build a lead.** Make each move do a job. Develop with a threat, so the opponent must answer instead of developing. Castle early. Early queen moves usually lose time unless each carries a threat. **Defend against one.** Develop a defender, trade the attacker, give the king a square. [I] Closing the centre may help, but the test position below is a case where capturing is best. Capablanca and Emanuel Lasker both urged bringing the pieces out quickly; see the sources.

steps.text: Nimzowitsch warned against pawn-grabbing while development is unfinished: "Never play to win a pawn while your development is yet unfinished!" (*My System*). He allowed one exception, a centre pawn taken without much danger. A gambit is the same trade seen from the other side: Emanuel Lasker described it as a pawn given for time and open lines. [I] The price is paid in tempi.

steps.caption: Black to move, one move before the first board. Two defences work (develop the king's knight, or open the bishop's diagonal with e6; depth 16). The pawn push of the first board gives White a sacrifice worth over three pawns. Defend by developing a defender or blocking the diagonal, not by chasing the bishop with a pawn.

steps.text: **What decided it.** Before the first sacrifice White had four pieces out and Black two, with a knight and a bishop at home. [I] Black's early bishop trade did not change the count, but the recapture put White's queen on f3 with tempo. After that nearly every White move carried a threat, while Black's replies developed little. Early queen moves are fine when each one makes a threat. Go back through the game and list which White moves threatened something.

steps.text: **What to remember.** Count pieces that do something, plus castling, on both sides. A lead is the difference. A sacrifice needs a lead, a target few pieces defend, and a king with no safe run. A developed defender or a safe king square cancels it. Waiting shrinks a lead. Build one with threats; defend one by trading the attacker.

**Self-check before you teach it.** Did you say when a lead works and when it fails? Did you give one example a beginner could set on a board? Did you name one mistake, such as grabbing a pawn or leaving a bishop to be fed a trap? Did you say what you counted and how? Say it in your own words; the app does not grade it.
